text: Every tool in this chapter — signature antivirus, EDR, a Linux agent — only protects assets it knows about. This lesson is about the gap underneath all of them: the devices nobody's tracking at all, and why finding them matters as much as any single security tool.

An asset that isn't tracked gets none of the protections from this chapter, by definition. IT can't push an EDR agent to a device it doesn't know exists, a patch management program can't patch a server that isn't on its list, and nobody is watching logs from a machine nobody registered. An untracked asset isn't neutral — it's pure attack surface, exposed to the same network as everything else but defended by nobody.

The usual fix is a configuration management database, or CMDB — a system of record listing every known hardware and software asset, along with its owner, operating system, patch level, and business criticality. Patch management, vulnerability scanning, and EDR deployment all draw their scope from that list: if a server isn't in the CMDB, most organizations' security tooling never even considers it a target to protect.

The problem is that a CMDB only reflects what's been entered into it, and nothing enforces that every new device gets added. A network discovery scan closes that gap from the other direction — nmap -sn 10.20.0.0/16 pings every address in a subnet to find what's actually alive on the network right now, and nmap -sV -O against a specific host fingerprints its running services and operating system once you've found it.

Comparing that scan result against the CMDB is where the real risk shows up. Anything the scan finds that the CMDB doesn't know about is shadow IT or a forgotten server — a test VM spun up for a project in 2022 and never decommissioned, say, still running an unpatched SQL Server two years later, quietly reachable from the rest of the internal network the whole time.

That gap between what a CMDB believes exists and what a discovery scan actually finds is where a lot of real breaches start — not a sophisticated exploit, just an asset nobody was watching.
